newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Restructure or die, EU warns defence industry.
newsitem.headline: Restructure or die, EU warns defence industry.

text.p: Europe's defence industry, squeezed by shrinking military budgets and tougher U.S. competition, must boost its competitiveness to survive, a senior European Commission official said on Tuesday.

Guy Crauser, deputy-director general of the Commission's division responsible for industry, said this to a large extent could only be done with "clear support" of EU member states both as the main customers and sometimes owners.

He was participating in a conference on Europe's defence industry at which the need to consolidate and restructure was a dominant theme, especially in view of increasingly stiff competition from U.S. defence giants.

As a result of drastic cuts in national defence budgets, the number of people directly employed in Europe's defence industry has been halved to around 600,000 in the last decade. Despite this, the sector remains fragmented in the European Union.
In contrast, U.S. rivals have responded quickly to the post-Cold War era by forcefully restructuring their industry.
Crauser said the pace of change in the U.S. industry left Europe with no choice but to restructure, including possible privatisations and mergers.

"Until now the European defence industry has not been able to provide an adequate response to the decline in armaments expenditure and the rapid restructuring of the U.S. defence industry," Crauser told the conference.

Unless bold political decisions were taken, the European defence and technological base would not withstand the triple pressure of declining defence budgets, increased U.S. and third country competition and national resistance to integration.
"It is now time to encourage the European defence industry to take the necessary steps to enhance its competitiveness, steps which are necessary for its sheer survival," he added.
Standardisation, competition policy and procurement rules could help boost the competitive power of Europe's defence industry, he said.
Crauser did not mention recent events in France, but the prospects for industry consolidation in Europe have become more uncertain following the Socialists' election victory this month.
The previous government was preparing to privatise state-controlled defence electronics firm Thomson-CSF, but the deal has now been put on hold.
Crauser's views on the necessity for restructuring were echoed by other participants.

Sir Geoffrey Pattie, chairman of GEC-Marconi, a division of Britain's General Electric Co Plc, warned that the defence industry could be "wiped out" if Europe failed to meet the structural challenges ahead. He complained that there were hardly any world class European aerospace companies.

"The problem of course is that we can't go out and merge like the United States companies are doing so spectacularly because of the regulatory framework and the fact that we are all working for different countries," Pattie said.
Roger Hawksworth, deputy chief executive of Matra-BAe Dynamics, said the consolidation of the industry was not simply urgent, but overdue.

"The consequences of inaction now will be a major erosion of Europe's position in world civil and defence aerospace markets," he warned. "Europe can find itself very quickly being reduced to a niche player with an increasingly limited technology base."

Hawksworth said Europe must award key defence programmes to its own industry if it wished to remain an alternative to the U.S. industry. "Of course the European industry must be fit enough and competitive enough to win -- no free lunch."
His firm is a joint venture between France's Lagardere and British Aerospace, formed after lengthy cross-border negotiations.

"We are still in the early stages of consolidation in Europe. It is clearly important that those of us in the forefront of the process do not get penalised by our governments for ceasing to be wholly British or wholly French," he said.
